## Compute Dispersion


## import dataset with all gradients

```{r}
combined_gradients <- pc_read_gradients(c("rs2", "rs3"), data_root = paths$data_root) %>%
  select(NECOS_ID, scan, parcel, V1, V2, V3)

# Load and process IV dataframe
IV <- pc_mean_fd(paths$data_root, scans = c("rest2", "rest3")) %>%
  select(NECOS_ID, scan, headmotion, stress = Group)

parcel_labels <- pc_parcel_labels(paths$data_root) %>%
  select(X7networks_order,X7networks)%>%
  rename(parcel = X7networks_order)


# Merging the gradients data with IV
final_data <- merge(IV, combined_gradients, by = c("NECOS_ID", "scan"))
final_data <- merge(parcel_labels[c("parcel", "X7networks")], final_data, by = c("parcel"))

pc_write_csv(final_data, file.path(tables_dir, "dispersion_gradients_parcel_labels_iv.csv"))

```

## create the centroid dataset

calculate the centroid of the network as the mean of all parcels in the 3D space
```{r}
# Next we calculate the centroid for each network based on its corresponding parcels

library(dplyr)

mean_centroids <- final_data %>%
  group_by(NECOS_ID, X7networks, scan) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_V1 = mean(V1, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_V2 = mean(V2, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_V3 = mean(V3, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
pc_write_csv(mean_centroids, file.path(tables_dir, "dispersion_mean_centroids.csv"))


```
## Compute the distance between the centroids of the salience, control, and control network per participant

```{r}

# Assuming the networks are named as 'Default', 'Control', and 'Salience'
networks <- c("Default", "Control", "Salience")

# Replace "Salience / Ventral Attn" with "Salience" in the X7networks column
mean_centroids <- mean_centroids %>%
  mutate(X7networks = ifelse(X7networks == "Salience / Ventral Attn", "Salience", X7networks))

# Filter to keep only relevant networks
filtered_data <- mean_centroids %>%
  filter(X7networks %in% networks)

# Pivot and reshape the data
wide_data <- filtered_data %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = X7networks, values_from = c(mean_V1, mean_V2, mean_V3))

# Compute Euclidean distance for each participant and resting state
euclidean_distances <- wide_data %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(
    distance_default_control = sqrt(sum((c(mean_V1_Default, mean_V2_Default, mean_V3_Default) - 
                                          c(mean_V1_Control, mean_V2_Control, mean_V3_Control))^2)),
    distance_default_salience = sqrt(sum((c(mean_V1_Default, mean_V2_Default, mean_V3_Default) - 
                                           c(mean_V1_Salience, mean_V2_Salience, mean_V3_Salience))^2)),
    distance_control_salience = sqrt(sum((c(mean_V1_Control, mean_V2_Control, mean_V3_Control) - 
                                           c(mean_V1_Salience, mean_V2_Salience, mean_V3_Salience))^2))
  ) %>%
  select(NECOS_ID, scan, distance_default_control, distance_default_salience, distance_control_salience)


# Merge IV and euclidean_distances dataframes by "NECOS_ID" and "scan"
euclidean_distances <- merge(IV, euclidean_distances, by = c("NECOS_ID", "scan"))

# Write the resulting euclidean_distances dataframe to a CSV file
pc_write_csv(euclidean_distances, file.path(tables_dir, "dispersion_mean_between_distances.csv"))
```

### 1. Normality assumption of the dependent variable

**a. histogram**

```{r}
# Function to create and save histogram
create_save_histogram <- function(data, distance_column, title_prefix, file_prefix, scan) {
  # Create histogram plot
  p <- ggplot(data, aes_string(x = distance_column)) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "blue", color = "black") +
    ggtitle(paste(title_prefix, " - ", distance_column, " - Scan: ", scan)) +
    xlab("Distance") +
    ylab("Frequency")

  # Construct file path
  file_path <- file.path(diag_hist_dir, paste0(file_prefix, "_", distance_column, "_", scan, ".svg"))

  # Save the plot
  ggsave(filename = file_path, plot = p, width = 10, height = 8, device = "svg")
}

# Distance types to plot
distance_types <- c("distance_default_control", "distance_default_salience", "distance_control_salience")

# Create and save histograms for each distance type and resting state in euclidean_distances
for(scan in unique(euclidean_distances$scan)) {
  for(distance in distance_types) {
    subset_data <- euclidean_distances[euclidean_distances$scan == scan, ]
    create_save_histogram(subset_data, distance, 
                          "Mean Distances", "mean_distances", scan)
  }
}


```

### 2. Define model

Define 3 models of the same type with different dependent variables (between distance of centroids)
## between network dispersion
```{r}

# Function to run the model using afex::mixed
run_model <- function(distance_variable) {
  # Construct the formula
  model_formula <- as.formula(paste(distance_variable, "~ stress * scan + headmotion + (1 | NECOS_ID)"))

  # Fit the mixed model using afex::mixed
  afex_model <- mixed(model_formula, data = euclidean_distances)
  

  return(afex_model)
}

# Function to run the model using afex::mixed
lmer_run_model <- function(distance_variable) {
  # Construct the formula
  model_formula <- as.formula(paste(distance_variable, "~ stress * scan + headmotion + (1 | NECOS_ID)"))

  # Fit the mixed model using afex::mixed
  lmer_model <- lme4::lmer(model_formula, data = euclidean_distances)
  

  return(lmer_model)
}

# Run afex models for each distance measure
afex_model_default_control <- run_model("distance_default_control")
afex_model_default_salience <- run_model("distance_default_salience")
afex_model_control_salience <- run_model("distance_control_salience")

# run lmer models for each distance measure to compute plots easier later on
lmer_model_default_control <- lmer_run_model("distance_default_control")
lmer_model_default_salience <- lmer_run_model("distance_default_salience")
lmer_model_control_salience <- lmer_run_model("distance_control_salience")

# extract p-values of afex models
default_control <- afex_model_default_control$anova_table$`Pr(>F)`
default_control_p <- default_control[4]

default_salience <- afex_model_default_salience$anova_table$`Pr(>F)`
default_salience_p <- default_salience[4]

control_salience <- afex_model_control_salience$anova_table$`Pr(>F)`
control_salience_p <- control_salience[4]

# Extract p-values
p_values_interaction <- c(
  default_control_p,
  default_salience_p,
  control_salience_p
)

# Apply Bonferroni correction across all three p-values
adjusted_p_values <- p.adjust(p_values_interaction, method = "bonferroni")

# Create a data frame with results
p_value_df <- data.frame(
  Distance_Type = c("Default_Control", "Default_Salience", "Control_Salience"),
  P_Value = p_values_interaction,
  Adjusted_P_Value = adjusted_p_values
)
#save df
pc_write_csv(p_value_df, file.path(models_dir, "dispersion_between_network_pvalues.csv"))


# Function to extract relevant summary data from lmer models
extract_lmer_summary <- function(model) {
  summary_model <- summary(model)
  fixed_effects <- summary_model$coefficients
  random_effects_var <- as.data.frame(VarCorr(model))
  
  return(list(fixed_effects = fixed_effects, random_effects_var = random_effects_var))
}

# Extract summary data from each lmer model
summary_default_control <- extract_lmer_summary(lmer_model_default_control)
summary_default_salience <- extract_lmer_summary(lmer_model_default_salience)
summary_control_salience <- extract_lmer_summary(lmer_model_control_salience)

# Extract fixed effects data into separate data frames
fe_default_control_df <- as.data.frame(summary_default_control$fixed_effects)
fe_default_control_df$Model <- "Default_Control"

fe_default_salience_df <- as.data.frame(summary_default_salience$fixed_effects)
fe_default_salience_df$Model <- "Default_Salience"

fe_control_salience_df <- as.data.frame(summary_control_salience$fixed_effects)
fe_control_salience_df$Model <- "Control_Salience"

# Combine the fixed effects data frames
combined_fe_df <- rbind(fe_default_control_df, fe_default_salience_df, fe_control_salience_df)

# Add P_Value and Adjusted_P_Value columns
combined_fe_df$P_Value_Scan_Stress <- rep(p_values_interaction, each = nrow(combined_fe_df) / 3)
combined_fe_df$Adjusted_P_Value_Scan_Stress <- rep(adjusted_p_values, each = nrow(combined_fe_df) / 3)

# Save the combined data frame
pc_write_csv(combined_fe_df, file.path(models_dir, "dispersion_between_network_model_results.csv"))




```


### 3. Check model assumptions

**a. normality of residuals**

```{r }

# Function to create and save QQ plot for model residuals
create_save_qqplot_residuals <- function(lmer_model, distance_type, file_prefix, parent_dir) {
  # Extract residuals
  res <- residuals(lmer_model)

  # Create a data frame for plotting
  res_df <- data.frame(residuals = res)

  # Create QQ plot
  p <- ggplot(res_df, aes(sample = residuals)) +
    stat_qq() +
    stat_qq_line() +
    ggtitle(paste("Residuals QQ Plot - Distance Type:", distance_type)) +
    xlab("Theoretical Quantiles") +
    ylab("Sample Quantiles")

  # Construct file path
  file_path <- file.path(diag_qq_dir, paste0(file_prefix, "_", distance_type, ".svg"))

  # Save the plot
  ggsave(filename = file_path, plot = p, width = 10, height = 8, device = "svg")
}

# Create and save QQ plots for residuals of your models
create_save_qqplot_residuals(lmer_model_default_control, "default_control",
                             "residuals_qq",
                             parent_dir)
create_save_qqplot_residuals(lmer_model_default_salience, "default_salience",
                             "residuals_qq",
                             parent_dir)
create_save_qqplot_residuals(lmer_model_control_salience, "control_salience",
                             "residuals_qq",
                             parent_dir)

```

**b. homoscadicity**

```{r }
# Function to create and save scatter plots for assessing homoscedasticity
create_save_homoscedasticity_plot <- function(lmer_model, distance_type, file_prefix, parent_dir) {
  # Manually compute fitted values and residuals
  fitted_values <- predict(lmer_model)
  residuals <- resid(lmer_model)

  # Create a data frame for plotting
  df <- data.frame(Fitted = fitted_values, Residuals = residuals)

  # Create scatter plot
  p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = Fitted, y = Residuals)) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
    ggtitle(paste("Homoscedasticity Plot - Distance Type:", distance_type)) +
    xlab("Fitted Values") +
    ylab("Residuals")

  # Construct file path
  file_path <- file.path(diag_resid_dir, paste0(file_prefix, "_", distance_type, ".svg"))

  # Save the plot as SVG
  ggsave(filename = file_path, plot = p, width = 10, height = 8, device = "svg")
}

# Create and save homoscedasticity plots for your models
create_save_homoscedasticity_plot(lmer_model_default_control, "default_control",
                                  "homoscedasticity_plot",
                                  parent_dir)
create_save_homoscedasticity_plot(lmer_model_default_salience, "default_salience",
                                  "homoscedasticity_plot",
                                  parent_dir)
create_save_homoscedasticity_plot(lmer_model_control_salience, "control_salience",
                                  "homoscedasticity_plot",
                                  parent_dir)

```

**c. independence (auto-correlation of the residuals)**

If the p-value is less than 0.05, we can reject the null hypothesis and conclude that the residuals in this regression model are autocorrelated.

Autocorrelation of the residuals should be avoided. Hence, if the p-value if not significant we assume no autocorrelation.
The interpretation of the Durbin-Watson statistic is generally as follows:

    A value close to 2 indicates no autocorrelation.
    A value less than 2 suggests positive autocorrelation.
    A value greater than 2 suggests negative autocorrelation.


```{r }

# Apply Durbin-Watson test individually to each vector of residuals
dw_default_control <- durbinWatsonTest(residuals(lmer_model_default_control))
dw_default_salience <- durbinWatsonTest(residuals(lmer_model_default_salience))
dw_control_salience <- durbinWatsonTest(residuals(lmer_model_control_salience))

# Extract the Durbin-Watson statistic from each test result
dw_values <- c(dw_default_control, dw_default_salience, dw_control_salience)

#Create a data frame to compile the results

durbin_watson_df <- data.frame(
Model = c("Default_Control", "Default_Salience", "Control_Salience"),
Durbin_Watson_Statistic = dw_values
)
# Convert to a data frame
durbin_watson_df <- as.data.frame(durbin_watson_df)

# Save the data frame
pc_write_csv(durbin_watson_df, file.path(diagnostics_dir, "dispersion_between_network_durbin_watson.csv"))

```

**d. multi-collinearity: Variance Inflation Factor (VIF)**

In multiple regression, two or more predictor variables might be correlated with each other. This situation is referred as collinearity.

There is an extreme situation, called multicollinearity, where collinearity exists between three or more variables even if no pair of variables has a particularly high correlation. This means that there is redundancy between predictor variables.

In the presence of multicollinearity, the solution of the regression model becomes unstable.

For a given predictor (p), multicollinearity can assessed by computing a score called the variance inflation factor (or VIF), which measures how much the variance of a regression coefficient is inflated due to multicollinearity in the model.

The smallest possible value of VIF is one (absence of multicollinearity). As a rule of thumb, a VIF value that exceeds 5 or 10 indicates a problematic amount of collinearity (James et al. 2014).

References: James, Gareth, Daniela Witten, Trevor Hastie, and Robert Tibshirani. 2014. An Introduction to Statistical Learning: With Applications in R. Springer Publishing Company, Incorporated.

```{r }
# List of all lmer models
all_lmer_models <- list(
  control_salience = lmer_model_control_salience,
  default_control = lmer_model_default_control,
  default_salience = lmer_model_default_salience
)

# Applying VIF to each model
multicollinearity <- map(all_lmer_models, vif)

# Extracting names of terms from the first model

terms <- names(multicollinearity[[1]])

#Creating a dataframe

vif_df <- data.frame(Term = terms)

#Adding VIF values for each model to the dataframe

for (model_name in names(multicollinearity)) {
vif_df[[model_name]] <- multicollinearity[[model_name]]
}

pc_write_csv(vif_df, file.path(diagnostics_dir, "dispersion_between_network_vif.csv"))


```

### 4. Model comparison

Likelihood ratio tests are used to compare the goodness of fit of two statistical models. The LRT compares two hierarchically nested models to determine whether or not adding complexity to your model (i.e., adding more parameters) makes your model significantly more accurate. The "hierarchically nested models" simply means that the complex model differs only from the simpler (or "nested") model by the addition of one or more parameters.

The LRT compares the fuller model against the simpler model and indicates whether the additional parameters improve fit.

```{r }
# Function to run the reduced model (without interaction of stress and scan)
lmer_run_reduced_model <- function(distance_variable) {
    model_formula <- as.formula(paste(distance_variable, "~ stress + scan + headmotion + (1 | NECOS_ID)"))
    lmer_model <- lmer(model_formula, data = euclidean_distances)
    return(lmer_model)
}

# Reduced models
lmer_model_default_control_reduced <- lmer_run_reduced_model("distance_default_control")
lmer_model_default_salience_reduced <- lmer_run_reduced_model("distance_default_salience")
lmer_model_control_salience_reduced <- lmer_run_reduced_model("distance_control_salience")

#Perform Likelihood Ratio Tests (LRT)
lrt_default_control <- anova(lmer_model_default_control, lmer_model_default_control_reduced)
lrt_default_salience <- anova(lmer_model_default_salience, lmer_model_default_salience_reduced)
lrt_control_salience <- anova(lmer_model_control_salience, lmer_model_control_salience_reduced)

#Extract LRT results
lrt_results <- data.frame(
Model_Comparison = c("Default_Control", "Default_Salience", "Control_Salience"),
Chisq = c(lrt_default_control$Chisq[2], lrt_default_salience$Chisq[2], lrt_control_salience$Chisq[2]),
DF = c(lrt_default_control$Df[2], lrt_default_salience$Df[2], lrt_control_salience$Df[2]),
P_value = c(lrt_default_control$Pr[2], lrt_default_salience$Pr[2], lrt_control_salience$Pr[2]),
P_adjusted = p.adjust(c(lrt_default_control$Pr[2], lrt_default_salience$Pr[2], lrt_control_salience$Pr[2]))
)

#Save the data frame

pc_write_csv(lrt_results, file.path(models_dir, "dispersion_between_network_lrt.csv"))
```
